passage: Note for Damini's parents, craft hour. I drew a sample card on the board: one flower, five petals, a green stem. Damini studied it, then copied it stroke by stroke, counting petals under her breath. She did not stop there. In the corner she added a big orange sun with long rays, because, she said, her flower needed daylight. Vaibhav, at her table, asked if he could copy her sun. I said yes, and reminded him to give his own card something new. Tomorrow we colour the cards and Damini will write the name inside.

qa.q: What did the teacher draw on the board as the sample card?
qa.a: One flower with five petals and a green stem.

qa.q: What might Damini have been feeling when she added the big orange sun?
qa.a: She was probably pleased with her own idea. She gave a reason, that the flower needed daylight, which shows she wanted the card to be hers. 🙂

qa.q: What other approach could Damini try if she wanted a card that looks less like the sample, and why?
qa.a: She could sketch a few ideas on scrap paper first. Seeing different flowers side by side would help her pick one that suits the birthday child.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Damini's card?
qa.a: He sees a sun he would like to borrow, and her changes show him it is fine to copy a starting point and then add something new.

grounding: The child copies the teacher's flower sample and then adds her own sun, so the copy becomes a starting point.

passage: Monday. Tejas squeezed glitter glue all over his drawing of a cat, and it smeared into a silver puddle. He frowned and pushed the sheet away. Wednesday. He took a fresh sheet and drew the cat in pencil first. "Glue is last," he told Dilnaz, who sat next to him. Friday. On the card for Nani's birthday the cat stayed clean, and only the border sparkled. Dilnaz leaned over. "Can I do mine like that?" Tejas showed her the pencil, then the glue, in that order.

qa.q: What did Tejas draw on the fresh sheet before using any glue?
qa.a: He drew the cat in pencil first.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when the glitter glue smeared over his cat?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and upset, shown by his frown and by pushing the sheet away.

qa.q: What could Tejas do next time to learn about the glue without risking his card, and why?
qa.a: He could test the glitter glue on a scrap of paper first. He would see how far it spreads before putting it near his drawing.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see Tejas's new way of working?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees a neat, sparkling card and wants the same result, so asks to copy the order of pencil and then glue.

grounding: A smudged drawing leads the child to try pencil first on a fresh sheet and glitter only at the border, learning an order for materials.

passage: Asif sat on the verandah step of their village house with a sheet torn from his school notebook. "Amma, how do I write Happy Birthday?" His mother Chandrika wiped her hands and wrote the two words in big letters on another page. Asif put his finger under the H, looked, and copied it. Then he looked again for the A. One letter at a time. His B came out backwards, so he rubbed it out and tried again. When the last Y was done he held the card up to the evening light. "For Dadi," he said.

qa.q: Who wrote the words in big letters for Asif to copy?
qa.a: His mother Chandrika wrote them on another page.

qa.q: What might Asif be feeling as he holds the finished card up to the light?
qa.a: He is probably proud that he wrote every letter himself. He is also happy about giving it to Dadi.

qa.q: What other approach could Asif use for the spelling, and why might it work?
qa.a: He could sound out each part of the words with his mother, clapping the beats. Hearing the parts would help him choose the letters.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel while watching Asif copy the letters?
qa.a: She may feel patient and proud. She gave him the writing he could not do yet and let him do the copying himself.

grounding: A child asks his mother how to spell the greeting and copies her letters one at a time, so the adult supplies what he cannot yet do.

passage:
"It's ugly!" Kamal crumpled the paper into a ball.
"Kamal, that was your card for Ravi," said Damini Ma'am. "The flower leaned a little, that's all."
"It's crooked. I hate it."
"Would you like to try one more? I'll sit with you."
"No. I don't want to."
"Ravi's party is tomorrow."
"Then I won't give him one." Kamal folded his arms and turned to face the wall.
Damini Ma'am smoothed the ball flat and put it in her drawer. Kamal did not look.

qa.q: What did Kamal say about his drawing?
qa.a: He said it was ugly and crooked.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he crumpled the paper, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was disappointed and upset. He crumpled the card, folded his arms and turned to the wall, so the crooked flower mattered a lot to him.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help Kamal, and why?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher to help him draw a first line, or turn the leaning flower into a flower in the wind. Then the card would not have to be perfect to be finished.

qa.q: How does Damini Ma'am see the crooked flower, and why did she keep the paper?
qa.a: She sees a small lean, not a failure. Smoothing the paper and keeping it leaves a way open for Kamal to come back to it.

grounding: A crooked drawing makes the child crumple it and refuse another card, so the wish for a perfect result stops the effort.

passage: Monday. Manjula and Manoj both grabbed the red toy car and pulled. "Mine!" "No, mine!" Manjula ran to the teacher with her fists tight. The teacher listened to Manjula, then to Manoj, and said, "Manjula has it till the sand timer ends, then Manoj." Both nodded. Tuesday. The same car, the same tug. This time Manoj ran to the teacher first. Wednesday. Manoj turned the sand timer over himself. "Your turn after this," he told Manjula, and she waited by the shelf.

qa.q: Who ran to the teacher first on Tuesday?
qa.a: Manoj ran to the teacher first.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she ran to the teacher on Monday?
qa.a: She was angry and upset about losing the car, shown by her fists held tight and her shout of "Mine!"

qa.q: What other approach could Manjula and Manoj use so they do not always need the teacher, and why?
qa.a: They could agree on turns themselves, using the sand timer. Then each child gets the car and nobody has to wait for a judge.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the teacher's decision?
qa.a: He gets a turn after the timer, and the teacher listened to him too, so it feels fair. By Wednesday he uses the timer himself.

grounding: Two children quarrel over a toy car, one runs to the teacher who listens to both and settles it, so the adult acts as judge.

passage: On the third floor of a city flat block, Aditi and Gurpreet both wanted the wooden train. Gurpreet shouted, and Aditi shouted louder. Then she stopped and took a breath. "You have it now," she said. "I have it after lunch." Gurpreet hugged the train and thought about it. "Okay. But you can't ask before lunch." They shook hands like grown-ups. When Gurpreet's mother called them to eat, he passed the train over, and Aditi laid the track across the rug.

qa.q: What did Aditi offer Gurpreet?
qa.a: She said he could have the train now and she would have it after lunch.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have been feeling while he hugged the train and thought?
qa.a: He was torn. He wanted to keep it, but he was also tired of shouting and willing to wait for a turn.

qa.q: What other approach could settle a quarrel like this, and why?
qa.a: They could toss a coin or play with the train together. Either way each child gets a fair chance without more shouting.

qa.q: How might Aditi see the deal she made?
qa.a: Aditi gives up the first turn but knows the train is hers after lunch, so ending the shouting seems worth the wait to her.

grounding: A child bargains by splitting the time, which ends the shouting so each child gets a turn.

passage:
"Ujjwal, come play catch!" Abhinav called across the yard.
"No." Ujjwal sat on the bench with his arms crossed.
"Why not?"
"You know why." If he says sorry, then I forgive him, Ujjwal thought. He waited.
"Is it the pencil box?" said Abhinav. 
"Say the word."
"What word?"
Ujjwal turned his back. The bell rang and neither of them played. Next morning, at the water tap, Abhinav mumbled, "Sorry I broke your pencil box." Ujjwal grinned. "Okay. Now come play."

qa.q: What did Abhinav break?
qa.a: He broke Ujjwal's pencil box.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal waiting for, and how did he feel while he waited?
qa.a: He was waiting for Abhinav to say sorry. He felt hurt and stubborn, sitting with crossed arms and refusing to play.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ujjwal try, and why?
qa.a: He could tell Abhinav plainly what hurt him, or ask a teacher to help. Waiting for one exact word left Abhinav guessing.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when Ujjwal says "Say the word"?
qa.a: He is probably confused. He does not know which word Ujjwal means, so the quarrel drags on until the next morning.

grounding: A child holds a rigid if-then rule, that he forgives once sorry is said, and the quarrel drags on until the word is spoken.

passage: At the school play corner, Irfan's block tower fell when Mahima's elbow bumped it. Their voices went loud, and then Irfan turned his back and started sorting crayons as if nothing had happened. Mahima held out a block. "Irfan? Irfan?" He kept sorting. At snack time he sat at the far end of the mat. Mahima watched him with her mouth turned down and ate her banana slowly. Later she asked the teacher, "Why is Irfan not talking to me?" Irfan's tummy still felt tight.

qa.q: What did Irfan do after he turned his back?
qa.a: He started sorting crayons.

qa.q: What does Irfan's tight tummy suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was still hurt and upset. He pretended the fight was not there, but the feeling had not gone away.

qa.q: What could Irfan try instead of turning away, and why?
qa.a: He could say, "You knocked my tower and I felt sad," or ask the teacher to help. Saying it out loud gives the hurt somewhere to go.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Irfan's silence?
qa.a: She is puzzled and a little sad. She does not know what she did wrong, so she asks the teacher why Irfan will not talk to her.

grounding: A child ignores the fight and hopes it will go away, but the hurt stays and the friend is puzzled by the silence.

passage: In the colony park, Jahnavi and Kabir both wanted the yellow scooter, and their voices rose. Preeti called from the swing, "Toss a coin! Heads is Jahnavi, tails is Kabir." She found a coin in her pocket and flipped it. Tails. Kabir rode first, and Jahnavi grumbled but nodded. A week later Jahnavi and Preeti both wanted the same swing. Jahnavi held out her hand. "Let's toss a coin, like last time." Preeti grinned and gave her the coin to flip.

qa.q: Who suggested tossing a coin at the park?
qa.a: Preeti suggested it from the swing.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when the coin came up tails?
qa.a: She was disappointed, since she grumbled, but she accepted it and nodded.

qa.q: What other approach could Jahnavi and Kabir have used, and why?
qa.a: They could split the time, one after the other. Each child would be sure of a turn without leaving it to luck.

qa.q: How might Kabir feel about the coin toss?
qa.a: Kabir probably felt happy and pleased to ride first, and Kabir saw the toss as a fair way to decide. 🙂

grounding: A third child suggests tossing a coin and both accept, and the first child remembers the idea and uses it at the next quarrel.

passage: Monday. At the sandpit Rafiq stepped on Chetan's sand castle. "I'm not your friend anymore!" Chetan shouted, and he stomped off to the far side of the playground. Tuesday. Chetan sat alone on a swing at break time and watched Rafiq play with the others. Rafiq looked over once, then looked down. Chetan kicked at the ground. Wednesday. Rafiq came with a bucket. "Want to build another castle?" Chetan shrugged, then took the spade. They built it a little apart at first.

qa.q: What did Chetan shout at the sandpit?
qa.a: He shouted, "I'm not your friend anymore!"

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on Tuesday while he sat alone on the swing?
qa.a: He was lonely and probably a bit sorry too. He kicked at the ground while watching Rafiq play with the others.

qa.q: What could Chetan try next time he is angry, and why?
qa.a: He could take a breath and say, "I'm angry that you stepped on my castle." Then the fight might end without losing a day of play.

qa.q: How does Rafiq feel after Chetan shouts and stomps off?
qa.a: Rafiq is probably hurt and unsure. Rafiq looks over and then down on Tuesday, and only comes back with a bucket on Wednesday.

grounding: A child shouts he is no longer a friend and stomps off, which ends the fight for the moment but damages the friendship until the next day's play.
